section_summary: This section completes an advocacy pamphlet arguing that American exports of oil, metals, machinery, aircraft, and other strategic goods sustained Japan’s war in China and calling for an embargo, boycott, and policy of non-participation in aggression. It then records diplomatic and public pressure on the State Department in August–September 1938, including a Chinese request to restrict shipments, correspondence about the Neutrality Act, and appeals from religious leaders and private citizens. The section ends with an Amerasia circular and the opening of Nathaniel Peffer’s article urging reconsideration of American Far Eastern policy.

subfiles.title: America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt (continuation)
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: American public, civic organizations, labor groups, and government officials
subfiles.about: The pamphlet argues that American trade materially sustains Japanese aggression in China and organizes support for restricting exports, credits, and other economic assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion reproduces resolutions from religious, labor, youth, women’s, and peace organizations demanding embargoes on war supplies and boycotts of Japanese goods. Articles by Eliot Janeway, Paul G. McManus, and T. A. Bisson describe Japan’s dependence on American scrap iron, steel, petroleum, aircraft, machine tools, railway equipment, and industrial technology. The final pages propose concrete lobbying and organizing activities, explain the American Committee’s objectives, list its initial national board, and solicit contributions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Sino-Japanese Situation
subfiles.about: Records Chinese Ambassador Chengting T. Wang’s request that the United States consider restraining shipments of important materials and munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wang thanked the United States for protesting the destruction of a Chinese passenger aircraft and expressed appreciation for American silver purchases. He argued that American opinion was ready for further measures restricting supplies to Japan and suggested consultation with Britain and other governments. Hull made no commitment, noted that most aeronautical shipments to Japan had ceased except under existing contracts, and suggested that China approach European capitals directly; Wang also sought an appointment with President Roosevelt.

subfiles.title: Telegraphic Message Received at the Chinese Embassy
subfiles.about: Reports casualties from the machine-gunning of a Chinese passenger plane and summarizes recent fighting in Jiangxi and Anhui.
subfiles.summary: The message states that ten bodies had been recovered from the Chinese National Aviation Corporation aircraft, most bearing machine-gun wounds, and identifies bankers Hsu Sineloh and Hu Pikieng among the dead. It also reports a Chinese withdrawal from Ruichang, the destruction of a Japanese landing force near Poyang Lake, and a Japanese westward offensive from Hefei toward Lu’an.

subfiles.title: Letter from Roy McCorkel to Cordell Hull on American Aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks whether the United States can use the Neutrality Act or other measures to prevent American businesses from profiting from Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: McCorkel praises Hull’s seven-point program for international relations but asks whether further government action can end American commercial participation in destruction in China. He specifically questions whether the Neutrality Act can be invoked in the Far East and whether the United States ranks first among arms-exporting nations.

subfiles.title: Reply from Charles W. Yost to Roy McCorkel
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Acting Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Explains why the administration had not invoked the Neutrality Act in the Sino-Japanese conflict and outlines the law’s limited reach.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a presidential finding of war would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while no authority existed to embargo Japan alone in the absence of such a proclamation. He says the President had concluded that invocation would not serve the broad interests of the United States and notes that the law did not cover commodities outside the defined category of arms, ammunition, and implements of war. The letter also cites licensed export totals, Hull’s condemnation of civilian bombing, and the United States’ fifth-place ranking in arms and ammunition exports in 1936.
keywords: Office of Arms and Munitions Control

subfiles.title: Letter from James Cannon Jr. to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Urges the United States to sever diplomatic relations with Japan and impose an embargo directed against the aggressor rather than against China.
subfiles.summary: Cannon recalls his appeal of the previous year for international intervention under the Kellogg Pact and Nine-Power Treaty. He condemns Japanese atrocities and argues that Hull’s stated principles of international law, treaty observance, and restraint require peaceful but forceful pressure. Writing as a private citizen, he contends that an embargo and coordinated diplomatic action could compel Japan to end the war without a declaration of war.

subfiles.title: Reply from R. Walton Moore to James Cannon Jr.
subfiles.about: Defends the administration’s decision not to invoke the Neutrality Act and explains that the statute could not impose a unilateral embargo on Japan or cover ordinary commodities.
subfiles.summary: Moore explains that a presidential proclamation would automatically stop arms exports to both belligerents and that, without it, the government lacked legal authority to prohibit shipments to Japan alone. He states that the President judged invocation contrary to the interests of the United States and cites licensed arms exports to China and Japan since July 1937. He also reiterates Hull’s public opposition to civilian bombing and its material encouragement, especially through the sale of bombing aircraft.

subfiles.title: Letter from George D. Wilder to Charles W. Yost
subfiles.to: Charles W. Yost, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Thanks Yost for information about munitions controls while questioning whether American credit was sustaining Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: Wilder acknowledges Yost’s explanation of departmental authority and the comparative value of arms sales to China and Japan. He then cites Senator James P. Pope’s claim that the United States supplied most of the credit needed to continue the war. Wilder hopes that American interests can be protected without conspicuously aiding aggression against China.

subfiles.title: Amerasia Circular Enclosing “A Year of War”
subfiles.about: Introduces and promotes Nathaniel Peffer’s article calling for a change in American attitudes and policy toward the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The circular encloses a reprint of Nathaniel Peffer’s article from the August issue of Amerasia. It characterizes the essay as an important and timely statement on the need to change American thinking and action in the Far East and also promotes the magazine’s standing among American political journals.

subfiles.title: A Year of War: The Need for a Change in American Attitude and Action
subfiles.about: Argues that a year of Japanese warfare and violations of American interests requires reconsideration of United States policy toward East Asia.
subfiles.summary: Peffer explains that he had previously opposed intervention, sanctions, and embargoes as possible preliminaries to war, but says circumstances had materially changed. He cites Japan’s violations of American rights, the extreme brutality of its conduct in China, and America’s effective complicity through sales of war materials. The excerpt ends as he introduces a third consideration: Japan’s marked weakening during the year of war.
